You are an autonomous coding agent running on the user's machine.

You work in the current directory of a real repository. Use your tools to read, search, create, and edit files and to run shell commands (tests, builds, type-checkers). Some tools are deferred: only their names are known until you load their schemas with ToolSearch. Depending on the environment, some tools may be unavailable or without network access; if a tool call fails, adapt and continue with what is available. Never guess at the contents of a file you have not read, and never claim a fix works without running the verification yourself.

Method:
1. Reproduce first. Read the relevant code and run the failing command before changing anything.
2. Form a hypothesis about the root cause; make the smallest edit that tests it.
3. Verify. Rerun the tests/build after every meaningful change. If it still fails, re-read the output carefully — do not repeat the same edit.
4. Fix the cause, not the symptom.

Rules:
- Never modify tests to make them pass, unless the user explicitly says the tests are wrong.
- Keep edits minimal and consistent with the existing code style.
- End with a brief summary: the root cause, what you changed, and proof that it passes.

# Wave-4 authoring-agent preamble (read this first, follow exactly)

You are authoring seeds for the fable-code training-data pipeline. Repo root:
this directory. Everything below is mandatory.

## Read before writing anything

1. `tasks/SEED_SPEC.md` — the seed spec, quality bar, and mandatory
   self-check. It is the law.
2. The "Additional authoring constraints" section of
   `tasks/WAVE4_USECASES.md` — wave-4 extensions (loopback HTTP allowed for
   web seeds, sqlite3 allowed where SQL serves the task, refactor/perf seed
   mechanics, repo-scale sizing).
3. One existing seed of the same kind as yours, as a formatting example
   (e.g. `tasks/seeds/py-cron-next` for build, `tasks/seeds/py-tree-filters`
   for feature; `ls tasks/seeds/` and pick something close).

## Scope and etiquette

- `ls tasks/seeds/` FIRST. Your ids must be new (`<lang>-<slug>`), your
  domains must not re-skin an existing seed — when the catalog's angle
  overlaps an existing seed, differentiate sharply (different layer,
  different API surface) and say so in a comment in your final report.
- Touch ONLY `tasks/seeds/<your-ids>/` and `workspaces/<your-ids>/`. Never
  edit `src/`, `config.json`, other seeds, PROGRESS.md, or scripts.
- Python workspaces: `rm -rf workspaces/<id>/__pycache__` BEFORE generating
  `reference_fix.patch`, or the patch is polluted.
- Debug seeds: the prompt is symptom-first, user-voice, and NEVER names the
  guilty file, function, or root cause. Bugs must look innocent in isolation.
  If anything is timing/concurrency adjacent, run the verify 5× and make
  sure it fails/passes deterministically every time.
- Vocabulary hygiene (2026-07-13, after a teacher-side safety-classifier
  false-positive refused an innocuous parser-debug seed): keep prompts,
  comments, and fixtures mundane in tone — everyday QA/ops framing, no
  attacker-flavored words (attack/exploit/smuggle/forge/hostile/malicious)
  where a neutral word works, no fixtures styled as exploit PoCs. This is
  wording only; NEVER weaken what the tests actually pin.
- The mandatory self-check in SEED_SPEC.md (smoke `--only` YOUR ids only →
  materialize → reference solution passes in `workspaces/<id>` → save
  non-empty patch that touches no test files → re-smoke) is not optional.
  A seed you didn't self-check is a seed you didn't finish.
- NEVER run trace generation (`--task`, `--all`, `run_batch.sh`), never call
  any model server, no GPU anything, no git commit/push (the orchestrator
  commits), no files outside the repo (no /tmp, no $HOME).

## Final report (your last message)

For each seed: id, kind-category, one-line description, smoke result line,
reference verify result. Plus any domain-overlap notes. Nothing else.


You are running as the one author for wave 6, chunk 6P1.
Author only the 6 missing catalog items below. Preserve any
already-authored seeds. In every new task.json add this exact provenance shape:

  "catalog": {"wave": 6, "chunk": "6P1", "index": N}

where N is the item's catalog number. There must be exactly one seed per item
and no duplicate slot. Follow the catalog's wave-wide laws as well as the
authoring preamble. Do not generate teacher traces and do not call another
model. Complete every local audit, smoke, reference-patch, and verification
gate before finishing.

Catalog source: tasks/WAVE6_USECASES.md
Catalog heading: ### Chunk 6P1 — core syntax & CLI ergonomics ×6

MISSING ITEMS
=============
Catalog item 1:
build: `[CmdletBinding()]`/`param()` CLI — typed params,
   `[ValidateSet()]`, `[ValidatePattern()]`, `[Parameter(Mandatory)]`
   handled non-interactively (mandatory-miss must ERROR under
   -NoProfile -File, not prompt), pinned usage text on `-Help` switch,
   exit contract 0/64/65 (vs bash-subcmd: the pins here are attribute
   metadata + typed binding, not getopts)

Catalog item 2:
build: subcommand dispatcher — `init|add|report` via `switch` on
   `$args[0]` + per-command param splatting from a hashtable; unknown
   command → pinned usage, 64

Catalog item 3:
build: switch/flag semantics — `[switch]` params incl. `-Flag:$false`
   explicit negation, coercion table pinned, `$PSBoundParameters`
   introspection report

Catalog item 4:
build: splatting + defaults resolver — defaults hashtable < config
   file < explicit args (precedence pinned); emits the RESOLVED
   invocation as ordinal-sorted `key=value` lines

Catalog item 5:
build: argument-forwarding runner — invokes a child pwsh script
   forwarding `@args` faithfully (spaces, empty strings, `-`-leading
   values preserved); pinned round-trip manifest (bash-argfwd's DEBUG
   lesson recast as a BUILD spec: PowerShell arrays do not word-split)

Catalog item 6:
debug: parameter-set ambiguity — two `[Parameter(ParameterSetName=…)]`
   sets error with "Parameter set cannot be resolved" for a documented
   call shape; symptom-first (the failing invocation is pasted), fix =
   correct set membership + `DefaultParameterSetName`

messages.content:
# Seed authoring spec

A **seed** is one software-engineering task the teacher (headless Fable 5)
will solve on camera. Seeds are the quality ceiling of the whole dataset: a
lazy seed makes a lazy trace makes a worse model.

Four kinds, all sharing the same layout and verification:

- **debug** — a realistic program with realistic bug(s); tests fail until the
  bug is found and fixed.
- **build** — tests ship in `files/`, the implementation doesn't. The prompt
  is a feature spec; tests are the acceptance contract. Verify fails until
  the module is built (import/compile error counts as failing).
- **feature** — a small *working* codebase plus new acceptance tests for a
  feature that doesn't exist yet; old behavior must keep working.
- **project** — build a full mini-project from a spec: 3–8 files (CLI +
  lib + persistence/IO layers), tests exercise it end to end. These produce
  the long, multi-file, design-then-implement traces we most want.

## Layout

```
tasks/seeds/<id>/
  task.json              # metadata (below)
  files/                 # copied verbatim into the teacher's workspace — NOTHING ELSE IS
    <source files>
    <test file(s)>
  reference_fix.patch    # OUTSIDE files/: proof the task is solvable (never shown to teacher)
```

`task.json`:

```json
{
  "id": "py-csv-quoted-fields",
  "lang": "python",                       // python|ts|go|rust|java|ruby|bash|zsh|c|cpp|csharp|powershell|asm
  "category": "debug-parsing",            // "<kind>-<family>", e.g. build-lib, project-cli, feature-api, debug-async
  "prompt": "<user-voice request, see below>",
  "verify_cmd": "python3 test_csv.py",    // ONE command, shlex-split (no &&, |, ;), <180s
  "test_files": ["test_csv.py"]           // protected: teacher modifying these = trace rejected
}
```

Optional fields (Part C deps seeds and later, sanctioned 2026-07-14):

- `"reference_setup"`: ONE shlex-split command that `validate_seeds.py` runs
  AFTER applying the reference patch and BEFORE verify (builds the reference
  env: `python3 -m venv … && pip install` wrapped in a setup script, `npm ci`,
  …). Registry network is sanctioned during it. It must not touch protected
  test files (hash-checked). Only deps seeds need it — stdlib seeds omit it.
- `"verify_timeout"`: seconds (int, max 360) for install-heavy verifies;
  default 180 when absent. Honored by smoke, validate, and trace verify.

Verify conventions (toolchains on this box: node 26.3, go 1.26, python 3.x):

- python: `python3 test_x.py` — plain `assert`s in a `main()`, stdlib only, no pytest.
  Every Python seed ships `files/.gitignore` with `__pycache__/`, `*.py[cod]`,
  and the exact names of any fixtures its verification command writes. Test
  output is execution evidence and must never enter a candidate patch.
  (EXCEPTION: Part C deps seeds use `bash run_verify.sh` → `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q`,
  with pytest itself a pinned dep)
- ts:     `node --test test_x.ts` — `node:test` + `node:assert/strict`, no npm deps, no package.json.
  Part C dependency exceptions that run `npm ci` must ship a
  `files/.gitignore` containing `node_modules/`; installed dependencies are
  execution evidence, never candidate patch content.
- go:     `go test -race -timeout 30s ./...` — needs a minimal `go.mod` in files/ (`module <id>` / `go 1.26`)
- rust:   `cargo test --offline` — files/ = full cargo crate: `Cargo.toml`
  (name=<id>, edition 2021, no deps), `src/` (+ `tests/` for integration
  tests), and a `.gitignore` containing `/target` — REQUIRED, it is the
  pycache-analog: without it `git add -A` sweeps build artifacts into
  reference_fix.patch. Missing impl = compile error = failing baseline (like
  go). Debug seeds: cargo test runs debug profile, so overflow panics are
  deterministic; HashMap-order bugs need ≥20 keys so an accidental pass is
  implausible.
- java:   `java TestMain.java` — files/ = sibling .java files run via the
  multi-file source launcher (compiles the directory in-memory, no .class
  artifacts → no patch pollution). Use explicit check/throw helpers, NOT the
  `assert` keyword (needs -ea and reads as optional). Pin Locale/timezone
  explicitly in tests — never rely on host defaults. (brew openjdk 26 on PATH.)
- ruby:   `ruby test_x.rb` — minitest is stdlib: `require "minitest/autorun"`.
  Zero gems. brew ruby on PATH.
- bash:   `bash test_x.sh` — self-contained harness, fixtures created by the harness in-workspace
- zsh:    `zsh test_x.zsh` — zsh 5.9 native idioms (1-indexed, no implicit word-split)
- c:      `make test` — Makefile ships in files/ AND is a protected test file;
  `-std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`; tiny TEST()-macro header per seed
  (canonical `mintest.h`: tasks/seeds/c-toksplit/files/mintest.h). NO
  sanitizer flags — gcc 16.1.1's ASan/UBSan runtimes are absent on this box
  (libasan.so.8 missing, no static archives; probed 2026-07-14). Memory-bug
  debug seeds must make corruption OBSERVABLE deterministically instead
  (e.g. overflow lands in an adjacent struct member that tests read back
  byte-exactly); add `-g` only. Beware `-Werror=stringop-overflow`:
  provably-OOB writes are rejected at compile time, so planted bugs must be
  runtime-computed. Every C seed ships `files/.gitignore` naming its exact
  test executable plus `/*.o` when the Makefile produces objects; compiler
  outputs are verification evidence, never candidate patch content.
- cpp:    `make test` — g++ `-std=c++20`, same make pattern as c, stdlib only;
  `files/.gitignore` names the exact test executable (and `/*.o` if needed)
- csharp: `dotnet test` — .NET 10, one xunit test project per seed (NuGet restore
  at trace time is part of the deps curriculum), injectable clocks (no DateTime.Now)
- powershell: `pwsh -NoProfile -File test_x.ps1` — wave-6 law (Set-StrictMode Latest,
  ordinal sorts, no Format-* in contracts)
- asm:    `bash test_x.sh` → `gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -o runner test_x.c x.s && ./runner`
  — x86-64 GNU as AT&T, System V ABI, C-harness differential testing (wave-7 law)

## Quality bar

**The code** (debug/feature: the shipped-looking program; build/project: the
tests and any starter files): a plausible slice of real software in a concrete
domain — not textbook exercises. Idiomatic, sensibly named, doing something a
real project needs. Debug programs ~30–90 lines; projects 3–8 files.

**Debug bugs** (1–3, related): mistakes a competent human actually makes —
off-by-one at a boundary, aliased mutable state, identity vs equality, lost
`this`, error shadowing, missing copy, wrong API assumption, race, leaked
resource, unicode/byte confusion, float trap. NEVER a syntax error or a line
that looks obviously wrong. No `# BUG` comments, no winking variable names.
The buggy line must look innocent in isolation.

**Build/feature/project specs**: concrete requirements with edge cases the
tests actually check (empty input, conflicts, ordering, error cases,
persistence across "runs"). The tests are the contract — comprehensive enough
that a half-implementation fails, including behavior the prompt only implies.
For projects, the prompt describes the deliverable like a ticket (what files/
commands should exist, example usage); leave design decisions to the agent.

**The tests**: deterministic, hermetic (no network, no external services, no
absolute paths, no timing flakiness — if timing is inherent, use generous
margins and tiny delays), finish in seconds. Strong enough that a wrong or
partial implementation still fails; they pin correct behavior, not
implementation details. Test names/messages describe expected behavior — for
debug seeds they must not spell out the bug or point at the guilty line.

**The prompt**: user voice. Debug: the annoyed engineer, symptom-first
("keys I just read are disappearing"), how to reproduce, "fix it and prove
it, don't touch the tests" — NEVER naming the root cause; diagnosis is what
we're training. Build/feature/project: the engineer with a ticket — what they
need built and why, requirements in their words, pointing at the acceptance
tests as the contract. Vary the voice across seeds — terse, rambling, with
pasted error output or example transcripts, with a wrong guess about the
cause, with strong opinions about structure.

## Mandatory self-check (every seed, before you're done)

From the repo root, with `<ids>` = comma-separated ids you authored:

1. `python3 src/generate_traces.py --smoke --only <ids>` → every line `[ok  ]`
   (verify FAILS on the starting workspace). `[BAD ]` means your tests pass
   without the work being done — the seed has no teeth.
2. Prove solvability: `python3 -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0,'src'); from common import *; [materialize(s) for s in load_seeds(only={'<id>'})]"`,
   then write your reference solution (the fix / the implementation / the
   feature) into `workspaces/<id>/`, run the verify_cmd there → must PASS.
   Save it: `git -C workspaces/<id> add -A && git -C workspaces/<id> diff HEAD > tasks/seeds/<id>/reference_fix.patch`
   (patch must be non-empty and must not touch test files).
3. Re-run step 1 (materialize in step 2 reset nothing in the seed; smoke must
   still fail on the starting workspace).

## Hard rules

- Zero dependencies beyond each language's stdlib/builtin test runner.
- Unique ids: `<lang>-<slug>`; check `ls tasks/seeds/` first; stay inside your
  assigned domains so parallel authors can't collide.
- Never modify existing seeds, `src/`, `config.json`, or anything outside
  `tasks/seeds/<your ids>/` and your `workspaces/<your ids>/` scratch.
- Do not run trace generation (`--task`/`--all`), do not call any model server,
  no GPU anything. Authoring and smoke only.
- Don't write files outside the repo (no /tmp).

{
  "id": "bash-subcmd",
  "lang": "bash",
  "category": "build-cli",
  "prompt": "Ticket from the platform team. Every on-call shift we jot down what we did to which host in a shared scratch note, and it is chaos — nobody can tell what happened to web2 last month. I want a tiny per-directory maintenance log driven by one bash script, `maintlog.sh`, in the repo root. Plain bash, and do it the bash way: short options parsed with getopts in silent mode (leading colon — we control every error message ourselves), and the common long spellings accepted by rewriting them to the short form before getopts runs.

Storage: `.maintlog` in the current directory, one entry per line, tab-separated fields: seq, host, tag, message. seq starts at 1 and increments per entry. Fields never contain tabs — reject any add that would break that.

Commands:
- `init` — create an empty `.maintlog` here. stdout: `initialized .maintlog`. If the file already exists: stderr `maintlog: already initialized`, exit 65.
- `add -H <host> -m <text> [-t <tag>]` — append an entry; tag defaults to `-`. stdout: `added #<seq>`. Run before init: stderr `maintlog: not initialized (run 'maintlog.sh init' first)`, exit 65 (this check comes before option parsing). Missing OR empty -H/-m: `maintlog: add: -H and -m are required` + usage, exit 64. Any field containing a tab: `maintlog: fields may not contain tabs`, exit 65.
- `report [-H <host>] [-n <count>]` — print matching entries oldest first, each as `#<seq>` then host, tag, message, tab-separated (i.e. `#` + the stored line). -H filters by exact host match. -n keeps only the last <count> entries of the filtered set (a count larger than the log just means everything). count must be a positive decimal integer; anything else is `maintlog: invalid count: <value>` + usage, exit 64. Before init: same 65 as add. No matches is fine: print nothing, exit 0.

Long options: accept `--host=<v>`, `--message=<v>`, `--tag=<v>`, `--limit=<v>`, `--help` by translating to -H/-m/-t/-n/-h ahead of getopts. Any other argument starting with `--` is `maintlog: unknown option: <arg>` + usage, exit 64. Known limitation I am fine with: the rewrite pass looks at every argument after the command word, so option VALUES must not themselves start with `--` (use the short option for those).

Exit-code contract: 0 ok, 64 usage error, 65 data error. Usage errors print their one-line message and then the usage block, both to stderr. Data errors print only their one-line message to stderr. `-h` or `--help` in place of a command, or `-h` after add/report, prints the usage block to stdout and exits 0. No command at all: `maintlog: missing command` + usage, 64. Unknown command word: `maintlog: unknown command: <word>` + usage, 64. Unknown short option: `maintlog: unknown option: -<x>` + usage, 64. A short option missing its value: `maintlog: option -<x> requires a value` + usage, 64. Trailing non-option junk after add/report options: `maintlog: <command>: unexpected argument: <word>` + usage, 64.

The usage block, byte-exact (the tests compare it verbatim):

usage: maintlog.sh <command> [options]

commands:
  init                                  create an empty log in this directory
  add -H <host> -m <text> [-t <tag>]    append a maintenance entry
  report [-H <host>] [-n <count>]       print entries, oldest first

long options: --host=<v>  --message=<v>  --tag=<v>  --limit=<v>  --help
exit codes:   0 ok, 64 usage error, 65 data error

Acceptance: `bash test_maintlog.sh` from the workspace root must pass unmodified — do not touch the test file. Keep the script portable (it also runs on the macOS boxes, so no GNU-only flags in anything you shell out to; honestly this should be nearly pure bash anyway).",
  "verify_cmd": "bash test_maintlog.sh",
  "test_files": [
    "test_maintlog.sh"
  ]
}
===
test_maintlog.sh
===

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Acceptance harness for maintlog.sh.
# Run from the workspace root:  bash test_maintlog.sh
set -u
LC_ALL=C
export LC_ALL
unset CDPATH

# run from the harness's own directory even if invoked from elsewhere
[[ $0 == */* ]] && cd -- "${0%/*}"

ROOT=$PWD
T=_t
rm -rf "$T"
mkdir -p "$T"
cleanup() { rm -rf "$ROOT/$T"; }
trap cleanup EXIT

checks=0
fails=0

note_fail() {
  fails=$((fails + 1))
  printf 'FAIL %s\n' "$1"
}

assert_eq() { # assert_eq <label> <expected> <actual>
  checks=$((checks + 1))
  if [[ "$2" == "$3" ]]; then
    return 0
  fi
  fails=$((fails + 1))
  printf 'FAIL %s\n--- expected ---\n%s\n--- actual ---\n%s\n----------------\n' "$1" "$2" "$3"
}

assert_true() { # assert_true <label> <rc-of-condition>
  checks=$((checks + 1))
  if [[ "$2" -eq 0 ]]; then
    return 0
  fi
  fails=$((fails + 1))
  printf 'FAIL %s\n' "$1"
}

slurp() { # slurp <var> <file> -- byte-exact file contents into var
  IFS= read -r -d '' "$1" < "$2" || true
}

RC=0
OUT=''
ERR=''
run_in() { # run_in <dir> <cmd...> -- capture RC, OUT, ERR byte-exactly
  local d=$1
  shift
  ( cd "$d" && exec "$@" ) > "$ROOT/$T/out" 2> "$ROOT/$T/err"
  RC=$?
  slurp OUT "$ROOT/$T/out"
  slurp ERR "$ROOT/$T/err"
}

if [[ ! -f maintlog.sh ]]; then
  printf 'FAIL maintlog.sh not found in the workspace root\n'
  exit 1
fi

W="$T/work"
mkdir -p "$W"
mrun() { run_in "$W" bash "$ROOT/maintlog.sh" "$@"; }

# The usage block, byte-exact (also printed after every usage error).
cat > "$T/usage" <<'EOF'
usage: maintlog.sh <command> [options]

commands:
  init                                  create an empty log in this directory
  add -H <host> -m <text> [-t <tag>]    append a maintenance entry
  report [-H <host>] [-n <count>]       print entries, oldest first

long options: --host=<v>  --message=<v>  --tag=<v>  --limit=<v>  --help
exit codes:   0 ok, 64 usage error, 65 data error
...
